newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's NSW govt to sell betting agency.
newsitem.headline: Australia's NSW govt to sell betting agency.

text.p: The New South Wales (NSW) state government said on Tuesday it planned to sell off its TAB betting agency through a public share float.
"If caucus approves the proposal, during the next few months, the government will prepare the TAB for sale by public float," Premier Bob Carr said in a statement.
No figure was given for the value of the betting business but media reports have said the government expects to raise A$1 billion through the float.
Carr said the government would look to set aside a parcel of shares exclusively for New South Wales licenced clubs.
"The reduction in government debt which will follow the sale will save NSW taxpayers up to A$130 million a year," Carr said.
Treasurer Michael Egan said in the same statement the government would limit individual shareholding to five percent.

"By limiting each shareholding to five percent of the new TAB -- not just for the float, but thereafter -- we can ensure no one person or organisation controls the business and that ownership is spread through the community," Egan said.

NSW Minister for Racing Richard Face said in the joint statement that the owners of the new TAB will hold a 15 year exclusive licence to run off-course wagering in NSW and a non-exclusive licence for on-course betting.
Face said the government would give the operators of totalisator wagering the freedom to increase, but not decrease, pay-out rates, guaranteeing punters the same or better returns on their bets.
The government said it also endorsed a package of reforms for the NSW racing industry, which included cutting wagering tax by almost half.

The government said as part of the racing industry reforms a joint venture between the TAB and the industry will conduct off-course wagering in NSW. The venture will be 75 percent owned by the TAB and the rest owned by the racing industry.
It said the racing industry will receive at least A$165 million from its share of the joint venture's profits and contracts to provide racing products.
It said about A$50 million of racecourse development fund commitments will be paid out if the government receives sufficient excess above the reserve sale price.
